schema: if p, q; p; therefore q

example.text: If the first, then the second; but the first is, therefore the second is.
example.note: DL's schematic example, with ordinals for the propositions.

encoded.text: if p, q; p; therefore q
if p, q; p; r; therefore q
if p, q; p; p; therefore q

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.80 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: The first kind of indemonstrable statement is that in which the whole argument is constructed of a hypothetical proposition and the clause with which the hypothetical proposition begins, while the final clause is the conclusion; as e.g. “If the first, then the second; but the first is, therefore the second is.”
provenance.notes:
Same chunk (7.79): "As to the number of these, authorities differ;
Chrysippus makes them five." Concrete instances of the same form, all in
DL VII Hicks: "If it is day, it is light; but it is day, therefore it is
light" (7.76, chunk 0b12119b-5019-4600-98b9-20bc2cc1139a); "If Dion walks,
then Dion is in motion; but Dion is walking, therefore Dion is in motion",
given as the example of a syllogistic argument (7.78, chunk
f9d254ff-01b0-4b37-b98d-9d71132839a9); "If virtue does good, vice does
harm; but virtue does good, therefore vice does harm", given as a true
argument (7.79, same chunk). The mixed form "If Plato is alive, he
breathes; but the first is true, therefore the second is true" (7.77,
same chunk) is the logotropos, the same form with numerals in the minor
premise and conclusion. Also corroborated by Arnold, Roman Stoicism §162
(scholarship, chunk 35f286cd-cf33-400a-80e0-417dce60038c) and by Cicero,
Academica II, who calls it "the first mood" (see S010).

schema: if p, q; not q; therefore not p

example.text: If it is day, it is light; but it is night, therefore it is not day.
example.note: The minor premise, 'it is night', is not the contradictory of 'it is light', though DL's next sentence says it is (see the ledger notes).

if p, q; not q; r; therefore not p
if p, q; not q; not q; therefore not p

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.80 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: The second is that which employs a hypothetical proposition and the contradictory of the consequent, while the conclusion is the contradictory of the antecedent; e.g. “If it is day, it is light; but it is night, therefore it is not day.” Here the minor premiss is the contradictory of the consequent; the conclusion the contradictory of the antecedent.
provenance.notes:
In Hicks's example the minor premise is "it is night", which is not the
contradictory of the consequent "it is light", although the next sentence
says it is. The schema follows the definition, not the example. The
example should be checked against the Greek before this entry is used to
decide anything about contradictories versus contraries.
The definition uses "the contradictory" rather than "not". Whether an
argument like "if not p, q; not q; therefore p" (with the double negation
removed) counts as a second indemonstrable is a parameter question (see
rules.yaml C06, and Params.lean in Phase 2).

schema: not (p and q); p; therefore not q

example.text: It is not the case that Plato is both dead and alive; but he is dead, therefore Plato is not alive.

encoded.text: not (p and q); p; therefore not q
not (p and q); p; r; therefore not q
not (p and q); p; p; therefore not q

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.80 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: The third kind of indemonstrable employs a conjunction of negative propositions for major premiss and one of the conjoined propositions for minor premiss, concluding thence the contradictory of the remaining proposition; e.g. “It is not the case that Plato is both dead and alive; but he is dead, therefore Plato is not alive.”
provenance.notes:
Hicks says "a conjunction of negative propositions", but his own example
is a negated conjunction ("It is not the case that Plato is both dead and
alive"). The schema follows the example. Zeller n.230 (chunk
4b20ae16-4914-4fb8-9953-7b8efd451523) likewise reads the premise as "it is
not at the same time A and B", citing Diog. 80.
Mates (Mode 2 summary, chunk fcdf4b9c-1f28-4d6b-89a3-936a405e584e)
reports that the negated conjunction "leaves open the possibility that both
fail", and that one source (apparently Galen) held that no syllogism from a
negated conjunction is useful for demonstration. That is a dispute about
usefulness, not validity.

schema: if p, q; p; therefore r

example.text: If it is day, it is light; but it is day, therefore Dion walks.

encoded.text: if p, q; p; therefore r
if p, q; p; s; therefore r

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.77 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: Of arguments some are conclusive, others inconclusive. Inconclusive are such that the contradictory of the conclusion is not incompatible with combination of the premisses, as in the following: “If it is day, it is light; but it is day, therefore Dion walks.”
provenance.notes:
The conclusion is unconnected to the premises. The same example recurs at
7.79 as a false argument ("If it is day, it is light; but it is day,
therefore Dion is alive"), false because it is inconclusive (same chunk).
Mates's summary of Sextus's four kinds of invalidity (chunk
6dea256b-8bed-46db-9df4-e015a90e5636) lists "incoherent arguments (para
diartesin)", which fail because "premises bear no logical connection to
each other or to the conclusion". This example may be of that kind, but no
primary source in the corpus says so.
This passage is also the corpus's statement of the validity criterion:
see rules.yaml C08.

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.78 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: Arguments not syllogistic are those which plausibly resemble syllogistic arguments, but are not cogent proof; e.g. “If Dion is a horse, he is an animal; but Dion is not a horse, therefore he is not an animal.”
provenance.notes:
Denying the antecedent. Mates's summary (chunk
6dea256b-8bed-46db-9df4-e015a90e5636) reports Sextus's class of arguments
"propounded in an invalid schema (en asustatō schēmati)" and describes its
example as "affirming the consequent's negation while denying the
antecedent". That description is garbled in the summary and cannot be
matched to a schema without the Sextus text.

schema: 'p and q' is false; p; therefore not q

example.text: “It is both day and night” is false: “now it is day; therefore it is not night.”

encoded.text: 'p and q' is false; p; therefore not q
'p and q' is false; p; r; therefore not q
'p and q' is false; p; p; therefore not q

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.78 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: Of conclusive some are denoted by the common name of the whole class, “conclusive proper,” others are called syllogistic. The syllogistic are such as either do not admit of, or are reducible to such as do not admit of, immediate proof in respect of one or more of the premisses; e.g. “If Dion walks, then Dion is in motion; but Dion is walking, therefore Dion is in motion.” Conclusive specifically are those which draw conclusions, but not by syllogism; e.g. the statement “It is both day and night” is false: “now it is day; therefore it is not night.”
provenance.notes:
An important boundary case. DL calls this argument conclusive (valid) but
not syllogistic, so a correct reconstruction of the themata must NOT derive
it from the indemonstrables. Mates's summary (chunk
78c91994-ccd2-47ac-9eb9-17201baa0783) reads it the same way: the premise
says a conjunction "is false" rather than negating it, and "the Stoics
distinguished between the negation of a proposition and the assertion that
a proposition is false".
Ruling (Kyle, 2026-09-27): verdict valid_nonsyllogistic. The harness must
check both that the argument is valid under the validity criterion and
that it is not derivable through the themata.
Phase 2 represents "'p' is false" as its own operator (`saidFalse` in
Syntax.lean), semantically the negation but syntactically distinct, so no
indemonstrable applies to it. Lean/Stoic/Tests.lean proves that S008 is
valid under the criterion and not derivable from the base cases.

schema: if p, p; p; therefore p

example.text: If it shines, it shines: but it does shine, therefore it does shine?

encoded.text: if p, p; p; therefore p
if p, p; p; q; therefore p
if p, p; p; p; therefore p

provenance.source: Cicero, Academica II (Lucullus) ch. XXX (tr. C.D. Yonge, 1856)
provenance.passage: These are the arguments of Chrysippus, which even he himself did not refute. For what could he do with such a conclusion as this,—“If it shines, it shines: but it does shine, therefore it does shine?” He must give in; for the principle of the connexion compels you to grant the last proposition after you have once granted the first.
provenance.notes:
A duplicated argument (διφορούμενος). Zeller n.239 (chunk
8e7bb081-9d8b-481f-b3ac-57183751efa5, quoted in Zeller from Alex. Anal. Pr.
and Cic. Acad. ii. 30, 96): "Two such cases are distinguished, one in which
all three clauses, the other in which the conclusion and minor premiss are
identical. The first class are called διφορούμενοι· If it is day, it is
day; It is day, ∴ It is day." In the next chunk (
2ba79887-49fa-4618-8a50-f5c70d5cb00c, ch. XXX) Cicero adds: "I have learnt that everything which is
connected with itself is true". That is evidence that "if p, p" is a true
conditional (rules.yaml C01).
The Peripatetics objected to these arguments. Mates's summary (chunk
78c91994-ccd2-47ac-9eb9-17201baa0783) says they rejected "duplicated
arguments" and "tautologous inferences" because a genuine syllogism must
establish something not already known. The Stoic verdict is valid. The
Peripatetic objection is recorded here and does not change the verdict.
This form is an instance of S001 with q := p, so any reconstruction that
has S001 derives it. It serves as a sanity check, not a discriminator.

provenance.source: Cicero, Academica II (Lucullus) ch. XXX (tr. C.D. Yonge, 1856)
provenance.passage: What then do you think of this conclusion,—“If you say that the sun shines, and if you speak truth, therefore the sun does shine?” At all events you approve of the kind of argument, and you say that the conclusion has been most correctly inferred. Therefore, in teaching, you deliver that as the first mood in which to draw conclusions.
provenance.notes:
Yonge's English runs the conditional and the minor premise together. It
is read here as a first indemonstrable whose antecedent is a conjunction,
since Cicero calls it "the first mood". The Liar variant follows in the
same chunk: "If you say that you are a liar, and speak the truth, then you
are a liar. But you do say that you are a liar, and you do speak the truth,
therefore you are a liar." The form is not disputed there. The dispute is
whether the Liar's premises can be assented to.
This is a test of whether the object language lets an indemonstrable take
a compound as its antecedent.

provenance.source: Alexander of Aphrodisias, in APr., as reported in Zeller, The Stoics, Epicureans and Sceptics, ch. V n.239
provenance.passage: [239] Two such cases are distinguished, one in which all three clauses, the other in which the conclusion and minor premiss are identical. The first class are called διφορούμενοι· If it is day, it is day; It is day, ∴ It is day. The second class, ἀδιαφόρως περαίνοντες· It is either day or night; It is day, ∴ It is day. The latter term is, however, applied to both kinds. See Alex. Anal. Pr. 7, a; 53, b; Top. 7; Schol. in Arist. 294, b, 25; Cic. Acad. ii. 30, 96; Prantl, 476, 185.

non_primary.basis: ancient text quoted in a secondary work, not a primary edition

provenance.notes:
An indifferently concluding argument (ἀδιαφόρως περαίνων). Zeller's main
text (chunk 8026da9e-bbf9-4a39-b1e7-d2ca5604b7ca) says that among the
indemonstrable forms "importance is attached to some in which the same
sentence is repeated tautologically in the form of a conclusion". So the
Stoics accepted these arguments, and the verdict is valid on the Stoic
side.
This entry is in tension with the redundancy rule (S016). The disjunctive
premise does no work in reaching "p", yet the argument is not called
redundant. Any candidate that invalidates every argument with an idle
premise will reject this one. That makes it a strong discriminator between
readings of "redundant", and possibly evidence that redundancy was defined
relative to the premises' role rather than to derivability.
Ruling (Kyle, 2026-09-27): the conflict is not resolved. It is recorded
as finding F1 in NOTES.md, and redundancy becomes a parameter in
Params.lean. Under `strict` this argument is redundant and so invalid.
Under `narrow` indifferently concluding arguments are exempt, so it is
valid.
Mates's summary (chunk fcdf4b9c-1f28-4d6b-89a3-936a405e584e) uses
"adiaphorōs perainontes" for the transitivity arguments that Zeller calls
ἀμεθόδως περαίνοντες (n.232). That looks like a conflation in the summary.
Zeller is followed here because he quotes the terms in Greek.

Zeller n.245 (chunk 73ca2320-47fc-4eed-b9b0-fc8ad0d060e4) gives the Greek
name and the examples: "[245] Called μονολήμματοι συλλογισμοί. Such were

Plat. iii. 272, Oud."
That Chrysippus rejected them appears in the corpus only through Mates's
summary (chunk 78c91994-ccd2-47ac-9eb9-17201baa0783): "Chrysippus denied

Chrysippus's policy it becomes S001 with the conditional made explicit.

Phase 2 decision (Params.lean).

encoded.text: not (p and not q); not (q and not r); p; s; therefore r
not (p and not q); not (q and not r); p; p; therefore r

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.82 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: There are also certain insoluble arguments: the Veiled Men, the Concealed, Sorites, Horned Folk, the Nobodies. The Veiled is as follows: … “It cannot be that if two is few, three is not so likewise, nor that if two or three are few, four is not so; and so on up to ten. But two is few, therefore so also is ten.”
provenance.notes:
The Sorites. The " … " is in the chunk text itself. The corpus copy of
7.82 is abridged, so what DL says about the Veiled argument is lost.
Hicks's "It cannot be that if two is few, three is not so likewise" is
read as "not (two is few and three is not few)", a negated conjunction.
Each step is then a third indemonstrable followed by removal of a double
negation, which makes the form a test of the double negation parameter
(rules.yaml C06).
Chrysippus's response concerns assent, not form. Cicero, Academica II ch.
XXIX (chunk dc6299a6-98fb-450b-abd5-e19a5d96a49b): "For Chrysippus’s plan
is, when he is interrogated step by step (by way of giving an instance),
whether there are three, or few, or many, to rest a little before he comes
to the “many;”".
Ruling (Kyle, 2026-09-27): the chain form is valid, tagged kind: sophism.
The fault of the Sorites lies in its premises, not its form. Under the
syntactic reading of "contradictory" (C06), each link is a plain third
indemonstrable, since the contradictory of "not p2" is "p2". Under the
negation reading, each link also needs double-negation elimination.

provenance.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII 7.82 (tr. R.D. Hicks, 1925)
provenance.passage: The Nobody argument is an argument whose major premiss consists of an indefinite and a definite clause, followed by a minor premiss and conclusion; for example, “If anyone is here, he is not in Rhodes; but there is some one here, therefore there is not anyone in Rhodes.”
provenance.notes:
Listed by DL among the "insoluble arguments", that is, a sophism, which
is why the verdict is invalid. It has the surface shape of S001, but it
turns on indefinite pronouns ("anyone", "some one"), which a propositional
object language cannot represent. It is out of scope for the Phase 2
propositional encoding and kept as a warning: a string-level matcher would
wrongly classify it as a first indemonstrable. Chrysippus wrote on it
("Of the 'Nobody' Puzzle, addressed to Menecrates, eight books", DL VII
7.198, chunk a0776b89-9bed-4664-850c-7e4db6102c59).
Ruling (Kyle, 2026-09-27): removed from the formal suite, kept in the

provenance.source: Origen, Against Celsus VII.15 (tr. F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers IV, 1885), reporting the Stoics
provenance.passage: The concrete example which the Stoics give to illustrate this form of argument is the following: 1st, If you know that you are dead, you are dead; 2d, if you know that you are dead, you are not dead. And the conclusion is—“you do not know that you are dead.”
provenance.notes:
The "two conditionals" argument, the argument whose analysis the Phase 4
probes showed separates the candidates. Origen names the form just before
the example: "When, then, we find two processes of reasoning in both of
which the major premiss is the same, leading to two contradictory
conclusions, we use the form of argument called “the theorem of two
propositions,”". His Greek is in the translators' note 4700, which the
OCR of this copy garbles; it is the theorem "through two conditionals".
Two cautions. (1) The general schema sentence ("Of two things, if the
first is true, the second is true; 2d, if the first is true, the second
is not true, therefore the first is not true") is scrambled in this copy
by the OCR around note 4701, so it is not quoted; the schema above is
Crombie's sentence as it reads once the lines are put back in order.
(2) Note 4701: "We follow Bouhéreau and Valesius, who expunge the
negative particle in this clause." The printed schema rests on an
emendation of the Greek. The Stoic example does not depend on it.
Origen reports the form as Stoic; he is a hostile-neutral later witness,
not a Stoic, which caps confidence below the DL entries.
